explanation: Mandatory open-text questions are experienced as burdensome, deterring students who only want to make one point or provide a quick response.
quote: "why do i have to feel like nine different questions when i only want to give one point across?"

explanation: Students propose simple scaled questions with optional comments as a more manageable way to collect feedback without overwhelming respondents.
quote: "how do you feel on a scale of one to 10... tick, tick, tick and add optional comments"

explanation: Students suggest separating quick specific feedback from longer general feedback, using only a few yes/no questions and optional comments.
quote: "a more specific one that just has like, three or four yes or no questions. and then optional comments at the end"

explanation: Post-it notes and smiley/sad-face buttons are seen as accessible because they require little time and allow more students to participate.
quote: "posts posted notes were given out in the final lecture... the whole lecture to write it"; "just as you're leaving the hall have like a smiley face, a sad face"

explanation: Students criticise generic feedback forms because they do not focus attention on the specific course problems that need improvement.
quote: "all the feedback forms are very generic... 'what do you think we could do better?'"

code: Targeted feedback based on observed problems
explanation: Feedback is seen as more useful when linked to a clear observed issue, such as low lecture attendance or difficulty with coursework, rather than broad course impressions.
quote: "we are seeing like, a third of you turn up to lectures. is it because... lectures are not helpful, because you have too much work"

explanation: Students want feedback prompts tailored to the actual course and its current issues, helping comments relate to clear learning and course goals.
quote: "the feedback was like, tailored to the course... based on what they've seen"

explanation: A student compares weaker courses against a better-organised course and suggests staff learn from its structure, implying the need for shared standards of quality.
quote: "one of the courses... really well organized... maybe those sort of copy the other one... see how they're organizing, for example, the learn page"

explanation: Students report inconsistency in whether and how courses feed back to students about survey results, undermining reliability across the programme.
quote: "it really varies on how much they then fed back to us about the feedback that was given"

explanation: Students propose that someone outside the course review feedback to reduce defensiveness or conflict of interest and create a more reliable response process.
quote: "it might be good to have those be looked at by people outside of the course you can look at it more objectively"

explanation: Students question whether their feedback can influence a large, complex university system, which reduces perceived value of giving feedback. This is not directly about the qualities of feedback listed, so is coded as undefined.
quote: "the university is a quite complex and enormous system. and me... a few words from me and my classmates will not make a big change sometimes... i think like a few words from the students will not probably... the university will not be listening."

explanation: Students distinguish useful specific feedback prompts from broad general ones; specific questions help them focus on concrete aspects such as a lecture, topic, or explanation.
quote: "specific questions are more like, how do you feel about like lecture three? or, how do you feel about the professor's... explanations for a specific topic?"

explanation: Broad programme-level or general surveys are experienced as harder to respond to because they require students to think across multiple courses rather than against a clearly bounded object of feedback.
quote: "it's just, i guess, a bit harder to track down... when you have to think about different courses. it makes it a bit harder... than if they're just asking about one specific topic."

explanation: Students prefer feedback mechanisms that are easy to complete, using scales or choices first, with optional free-text for elaboration. This makes the feedback process more manageable and accessible.
quote: "it's always easier when there's like different options, or just to have to point and choose, rather than having to write loads... and then put the box for text."
subtheme: Low-effort structured formats with optional elaboration

explanation: A student suggests Likert scales or sliders with optional text as a more user-friendly design than open-ended text-heavy surveys.
quote: "i would put more like, likert scales, where you just have to choose or slide. and then if the respondent wants to answer more, they can just do that in the text box."
subtheme: Low-effort structured formats with optional elaboration

explanation: Long questionnaires discourage participation because they become boring or too time-consuming, even if they may collect more detail.
quote: "sometimes the questionnaire is like too long... there are like, so many pages... you can fill the form for like five minutes... i don't know why they designed it to be that long."

explanation: Mid-semester feedback is valued because there is still time for staff to respond and improve the course while current students can benefit.
quote: "they did was send a form mid-semester... 'in case, there's anything that we can fix, and try and do it better for the rest of the semester'... there's still time to fix it."

explanation: Feedback collected at the end of the semester is seen as less useful because it cannot resolve current problems for the students giving it.
quote: "a lot of the forms come when the semester is already ending. so that won't help us to solve the ongoing problem with the course."

explanation: Students are less motivated to provide detailed feedback when they will not personally benefit, such as when the course or degree is ending.
quote: "if the questionnaire is at, like, the end of the semester, i will be like less willing to give a lot more because it will not give me much benefit."
subtheme: Personal relevance and motivation to contribute

explanation: Students want acknowledgement of what was heard and what will happen next, so feedback feels visible and purposeful rather than disappearing into the system.
quote: "in a lot of cases, when they gather feedback, they're not like, oh, this is what people said. so we're going to try and do that. which i think, it would be helpful to know that we are being listened to."

explanation: The participant became motivated to provide feedback after experiencing repeated unsuccessful referrals and wanted to prevent others facing the same situation.
quote: “i noticed that there was an option to have feedback. and i've been knocking on every door possible to actually do that… each time they sent me to someone… there was always, ‘we can't help you’, or oh, go to this person… and that was kind of a repetitive problem… i’m just here to make that just not happen again.”

code: Feedback forms are too long and inaccurate on time
explanation: A student avoids completing feedback because forms take longer than advertised, making the process burdensome and discouraging participation.
quote: “sometimes i just decide to skip them, because i know they're going to be too long… they always say, like five minutes, it will take you ten. if they said twenty minutes, then it will take you ages, so don't do it.”
subtheme: Reducing burden and respecting student time

explanation: Feedback tools are difficult to use on a smartphone, which reduces completion because students often give feedback while travelling or during downtime.
quote: “i use my phone to give feedback… there are many times that it’s not really smartphone friendly, the feedback form. so you cannot see it properly on the phone. so it is hard to read and everything. so i just give up many times because of that.”

explanation: Students are unsure who to contact when they have feedback or a problem, suggesting the feedback system is not transparent or accessible.
quote: “i'm always confused. where should i go to when i'm like having any feedback or anything? we do have programme representatives, we do have school representatives… but the whole concept of it doesn't really work.”

code: Feedback not passed on or acted upon
explanation: The student perceives that feedback often fails to move through the system and is not taken seriously, undermining confidence in the process.
quote: “even if you do give feedback, it doesn't go through most of the of the times. and also even if you say something necessarily it is not being taken care of, or nobody really cares what you're trying to say.”
subtheme: Ensuring feedback leads to visible change

explanation: A student representative describes difficulty collecting, balancing, and escalating feedback, with no clear authority or mechanism to act on it.
quote: “it’s a lengthy sort of process and really tedious… how you said that often when you do get something it's really difficult to follow through and like, make it happen… i still haven't had any concrete meetings with any sort of authority… i've spoken to my lecturer, but that's about it.”

code: Optional open feedback reduces substantive input
explanation: When the meaningful written feedback section is optional, students may only tick boxes and avoid giving detailed feedback, especially if they doubt it will be implemented.
quote: “we had the mid-semester feedback form… but that was very brief. and it was like, the actual bit about the feedback was optional. so i kinda didn't give that much… tick the ones that i can, and not actually do the full feedback because i thought it's easier speaking to someone than filling it and not seeing it implemented.”

explanation: A student with ADHD found being required to use email rather than receive in-person help created barriers and contributed to a missed course opportunity.
quote: “i have adhd… it's much easier for me to go physically into the office… communicating via emails… can be a fuss… they said, no, no, no, no, you have to email us… because of that, i actually ended up not having one course on my timetable at all, and it filled up.”

code: Anonymous forms lack visible recipient or outcome
explanation: The student does not know who receives online feedback or whether it is read, making the process opaque and reducing willingness to participate.
quote: “most of the time has been anonymous feedback to... who knows. i don't know who received the feedback, i don’t know if someone read the feedback. and i don't know what happened with the feedback because these are mostly automated forms.”

code: In-person feedback more likely to receive follow-up
explanation: Compared with online forms, in-person feedback was associated with some form of follow-up, suggesting that visible communication loops improve perceived effectiveness.
quote: “because these times they were in person, i think most of the time, there was a follow up after that, an email or something about what i say and what happened after. all the other times… online forms… i also never see something back.”

code: Feedback helps identify mistakes and improvement
explanation: Students describe useful academic feedback as explaining what was wrong, what was good, and how that supports future improvement.
quote: "to know why you made a mistake, what was good and so on, so that you can move forward, you can learn and improve"

explanation: Students want feedback opportunities soon enough to remember the experience, but with enough time for retrospection.
quote: "it shouldn’t be so far away that i do not remember my feedback... so there is a balance there"

explanation: Students are more willing to engage when the university explains why feedback is being requested and what it is intended to improve.
quote: "telling us why they want feedback on this particular thing and what they want to do with it, rather than just sending it out"

explanation: Identical forms across courses make feedback feel disconnected from the specific goals, structure, and experience of each course.
quote: "every school has almost the same feedback form... the only thing that changes is the name of the lectures and tutors"

explanation: Students become overwhelmed and less thoughtful when asked to complete multiple similar surveys, suggesting feedback should be concise and varied.
quote: "i tend to feel demotivated when going to the last one... i just click on the very satisfied satisfied options"

code: Peer comparison would make results visible
explanation: Students want to see aggregated responses from peers so the significance and scale of feedback becomes visible.
quote: "look at how many of your peers agreed with you on this... motivates the student to complete the actual survey"

explanation: Students question whether anyone reads their feedback, making the process feel opaque and reducing confidence in acting through formal channels.
quote: "we don't know, even if we fill it out whether somebody actually read it... because there is no follow up"

explanation: In-person dialogue can make students feel listened to because there is a clear recipient and immediate response.
quote: "complaining to your flatmates is a big thing. because at least then you know that they're listening... versus if it's face to face"

code: Repeated issues without change damage credibility
explanation: As a programme representative, the student sees the same problems raised yearly with no action or explanation, undermining the ongoing feedback cycle.
quote: "every year they're the same problems with the same courses, the same issues raised and nothing changes"

code: Need explanation when change is impossible
explanation: Students do not always expect immediate change, but want reasons for decisions so feedback creates dialogue rather than silence.
quote: "maybe give us some sort of justification of why they’re doing it this way... explaining why it stays the same way, or what they're going to do about it"

explanation: Students experience course feedback as ineffective when the university does not report back on what was heard or what will change, breaking the improvement cycle.
quote: "whenever we're going to give this feedback, it never comes back to us... there's nothing literally... they're experiencing the same problems again, and again"

code: Desire to see how feedback data is used
explanation: Students want feedback processes to be transparent, including access to collected data and how it is communicated to decision-makers.
quote: "i want to see how it's being used and what that means, and how that's being transmitted to the relevant people"

code: Closing the feedback loop via course email
explanation: A course-wide response to survey comments was valued because it showed staff had engaged with observable student input rather than simply collecting more feedback.
quote: "one course where they've responded to the feedback that was given in those surveys in an email to everyone on the course... a good way to kind of close the feedback loop"

code: Staff specify actions taken from feedback
explanation: Students valued feedback responses that identified concrete changes or planned actions arising from their comments.
quote: "the professors... saying, like, ‘oh, this is what we're working on for next year’, or like, ‘we took this into consideration this year’"

explanation: Feedback was seen as effective when students could observe changes during the same semester, while the course was still ongoing.
quote: "in the same semester, the feedback from the midterm surveys were implemented and we saw the difference"

explanation: Students distinguish between general references to feedback and clear, concrete explanation of what will happen as a result.
quote: "people like mention the feedback, just like in passing, but never like concretely happens they're going to be implemented"

explanation: A simple, immediate, low-burden method in tutorials was perceived as more accessible than standard online surveys.
quote: "in the tutorial, he gave us bits of paper, and we had to write down something that was good, something that was bad... anonymously give it to him again"

code: Low response rates blamed on students
explanation: Students felt staff complaints about low survey uptake ignored whether the feedback method itself was accessible or engaging.
quote: "maybe change the actual mode of feedback and then you’d get more instead of blaming people for not engaging in something that's not very engaging"

explanation: Students report that feedback requests often arrive when assignments or exams are due, reducing the chance to respond thoughtfully.
quote: "it's always when we have like a midterm essays are due this week, and they’re like, you have this week to complete the feedback"

code: Final course feedback should follow assessment feedback
explanation: Students want to evaluate a course after receiving assignment comments, so they can judge whether feedback on their work was useful for learning.
quote: "after we actually received the feedback, and have time to read through it and digest it... to know why you made a mistake, what was good and so on, so that you can move forward"

explanation: Students may receive an initial acknowledgement that issues are being discussed, but lack ongoing updates on progress.
quote: “there are some problems they're still pending. they say they're trying to figure this out, but i haven't heard back from that… how is it going on right now?”

explanation: When students give feedback and do not receive a response, they become less motivated to provide feedback in the future.
quote: “when sometimes i give feedback and did not hear back from them, i feel hopeless and less motivated to give feedback next time.”

explanation: When asked what they would change, students prioritised transparent communication about actions taken and interdepartmental or external coordination.
quote: “telling the students what effort has been done following feedback… like a transparent changes. basically, the communication between this department and that one or with the external companies such as lothian buses.”

explanation: The absence of detail about negotiations creates frustration and a sense of exclusion; students want evidence of progress because they are most affected.
quote: “we don't know, what we discussed about… what's in discussion, because obviously, the students are mostly affected by it… we don't get anything like that.”

explanation: Failure to respond to disability support emails is experienced as poor feedback/support practice; even an explanation would have been preferable.
quote: “i email a few times, but i did not receive any response. yeah, i feel disappointed… it would be better if they told me… they should tell the truth to me just at the first time”

explanation: After academic difficulty, staff responded quickly and the personal tutor provided kind, practical suggestions, making support usable and reassuring.
quote: “several staff, including my pt and the year administrators think i really need a hand and got in touch with me immediately… she didn't judge me… really very well helping me. give me suggestion about everything.”

explanation: Concerns about compulsory placements and associated costs were perceived as dismissed rather than addressed with practical support or alternatives.
quote: “we’re willing to do it but like there’s no way we can do it, without getting support from the school… just to do a placement just to graduate… something that we just don’t talk about to our professors”

code: Lack of feedback follow-up discourages future engagement
explanation: Repeated absence of response to feedback reduces motivation to keep giving feedback.
quote: “90% of that i also never see something back to understand what's happened with the feedback. and that's why i'm not willing, as i was at the beginning, to give more feedback anymore, because who knows?”

code: Evidence submitted but not meaningfully addressed
explanation: A student reports providing proof of a technical issue and grading discrepancies but receiving inadequate accountability or evidence-based resolution.
quote: “i noticed that the portal wasn't working… and i had proof of that… i gave more feedback, proof of the differences… i said, can i have proof of grading?… they're like, no, that's confidential… i don't know, there's a big lack of accountability.”

code: Student representatives without a feedback destination
explanation: Student representative systems are viewed as ineffective when there is no clear place to submit feedback beyond individual lecturers.
quote: “there's no point having student representatives… i've spoken to my classmates about what they feel… but there's no place to give that feedback. because if you're talking to your professor there’s only that much that they can do.”
subtheme: Clear ownership and routes for feedback

explanation: Feedback collected after a short course ends cannot benefit the students currently taking it, reducing its usefulness for improvement.
quote: “i have a 10 credit course that i do over five weeks. and the feedback for that is at the end of the course. so, i don't see the point, because i want you to change something in between the course so that it gets better for the rest of the 2, 3 weeks.”

explanation: A student reports that feedback from the previous year did not lead to changes for the next cohort, indicating a weak continuous improvement cycle.
quote: “this student who did the same course last year… had given feedback to the course as well… she was like, oh, it’s the same thing. nothing’s changed… well, what's the point of this feedback, then?”

code: Survey questions are vague and repetitive
explanation: Online feedback forms are seen as generic, with limited yes/no options and little tailoring to the specific subject or issue.
quote: “the online forms are not that good… i personally do not really like how vague they are… there's just like, yes, or no answers… they're mostly kind of the same… it’s like they’ve copy-pasted all the questions.”

code: No proof of action after surveys
explanation: Students want evidence that feedback has produced change, but currently feel there is no proof that anything was fixed or acted upon.
quote: “there's no follow up for those things, like, they do not prove or give you any proof of any type of… that they have fixed something, or maybe they have acted on or something… you're screaming into a void.”

code: Surveys do not ask about students’ real problems
explanation: Feedback mechanisms are perceived as based on institutional assumptions rather than the issues students actually need to raise.
quote: “when i'm filling this form… they are not asking the right questions. like, i have a problem. and it's not addressed there… the problems that the university thinks that we have. but not maybe with the problems that we actually have.”

code: Feedback pathways send students in circles
explanation: Students describe being passed between offices without clear ownership, making it hard to know where to direct specific feedback or complaints.
quote: “it's really hard to find out who you need to talk to… you kind of move around those places… it just takes ages to just find out who you need to talk to… you just don't know who you should talk to.”
subtheme: Clear ownership and routes for feedback

explanation: Students with disability-related questions describe being redirected rather than supported, creating barriers and loss of follow-through.
quote: “i tried to ask about this from the disability advisor, and she was like, that is not our problem, go to the potterrow info place… you do not do that, because… especially, i forgot about that.”

explanation: Students lack transparency about where feedback goes and who reads it, which affects trust in the feedback process.
quote: "i have no idea who will be seeing it... course organizers should have the priority to see this feedback because they are the ones who are organizing the whole course."

explanation: Students want clarity about who receives their feedback, but also worry that too much visibility may reduce honesty if they feel identifiable to lecturers.
quote: "maybe more transparency... could also help... if maybe in the feedback form, it would say, 'so this feedback is going to your lecturers'... maybe that will actually make students answer less... there's got to be a midpoint between transparency and also confidentiality."

explanation: Live word-cloud feedback is experienced as interesting because students can immediately see the collective results of their feedback.
quote: "it was done live on the class so we can all see what others think about the course... if we... send some word... the word will instantly pop up on the screen."

explanation: Students want their feedback to result in observable changes, not just data collection; this reflects a desire for feedback to be usable in improving the learning experience.
quote: "maybe that the feedback was actually... like what we were asking for was actually done and that we could see that."

explanation: When students need immediate or practical action, they bypass formal feedback forms and contact staff or discussion boards directly.
quote: "if i have, like, any urgent things that need to be fixed, i will just email the course organizer, or through some discussion board... i will just ask the question there."

explanation: A course gathered students' desired revision topics and then used the responses to decide what to revisit, creating concrete action from feedback.
quote: "it was more the specifics that... we all wanted to go into for the last remaining weeks... they were like, oh, most people voted for this. so we're gonna go over this again."

explanation: Students prefer feedback responses that identify concrete next steps or possible solutions rather than simply stating that a problem cannot be solved.
quote: "what we don't want to hear that is, 'we cannot solve this issue'... rather than like, 'in order to solve this issue, what you need to do is blah, blah, blah', or... 'what we are gonna do is probably solution one, solution two, solution three'."

explanation: Students describe the feedback loop as poor because they submit forms but rarely know what happened afterwards, limiting continuous improvement.
quote: "i think it's not great at the moment... we might share it, but then we don't know what's happening with it... if it's a form... i think rarely i've known what's actually done with that."

explanation: Course representatives are seen as a possible ongoing channel between students and lecturers, especially for issues students may not want to raise directly.
quote: "i feel that position is a good midpoint in between students and lecturers... maybe for those cases, i feel the student reps are useful like that midpoint."

explanation: Students note that if representatives pass feedback on, they should report back about what was shared and what action will follow, completing the feedback cycle.
quote: "if they told us back, oh, we've shared this and then they're gonna do this and this."

code: Conflict of interest in receiving criticism
explanation: Students identify a conflict when the person receiving critical feedback is also the person responsible for the course, which may affect how feedback is interpreted or acted upon.
quote: "there's definitely a conflict of interest there"; "someone who's maybe getting critiques on their own stuff... they'd be less inclined to change things"

explanation: Students note that feedback mechanisms often capture the views of those who attend and engage, while missing those who are struggling or absent.
quote: "the over representation is definitely in the people who turn up to everything"

explanation: Students who fall behind may stop attending feedback opportunities, meaning the voices most relevant to course improvement are overlooked.
quote: "because i'm behind on work, i don't necessarily go to those because it's not a priority... those are the ones that are actually struggling and might provide like better feedback"

explanation: Students worry that feedback can be linked back to them, particularly for personal or critical issues, affecting willingness to disclose concerns.
quote: "it wasn't necessarily anonymous... it could potentially get linked back to you... you might not say it"

explanation: Students feel uncomfortable giving negative feedback directly to the lecturer or staff member concerned, especially about teaching style or treatment.
quote: "sometimes it is uncomfortable to like, tell the person performing the course being like, this is how you're doing it wrong"

explanation: Students feel university feedback channels focus narrowly on lectures and workshops while excluding workload, wellbeing, and pastoral dimensions of learning.
quote: "the feedback that we are allowed to give from the survey to give us are always academic"

explanation: A student describes staff rejecting workload and mental health feedback as outside their responsibility, which students experience as a failure to recognise the source of learning problems.
quote: "people aren't feeling great about the workload. and the answer i got was, that's not our responsibility"

explanation: Students suggest focus groups or face-to-face conversations can make feedback feel more meaningful than online forms because concerns are heard by a person.
quote: "having like these kinds of discussions works better... you're actually raising your concerns to a person"

explanation: One student recognised that some changes had been made to the course over time, suggesting feedback can support iterative improvement.
quote: “i think they have implemented some of the feedback... i have seen some changes with past years... during our labs, i find that the labs are a bit better than they used to be.”

explanation: Students perceive departments as acting on some feedback while consistently disregarding other repeated concerns.
quote: “they are very, very selective in what they actually choose to change... feedback that has consistently, repeatedly... been an issue, that they have very, very consistently chosen to ignore.”

code: Mismatch between credit value and workload
explanation: Students describe a discrepancy between the formal goal or expectation of a 10-credit course and the actual workload required.
quote: “they justify it by, this is how much time we expect you to work on it... the reality is that it isn't actually true, in practice.”
subtheme: Alignment between stated expectations and lived workload

explanation: Students argue that accurate information about the nature and intensity of a course should be provided upfront so they understand what they are entering.
quote: “it's not advertised as such a huge component in the course... students should know what they're coming in for.”

explanation: A perceived gap exists between teaching staff’s estimation of required study time and students’ lived experience of the workload.
quote: “there seems to be... a discrepancy between the teaching staff’s impression of required hours, versus the student's actual experience of required hours.”
subtheme: Aligning staff assumptions with student realities

explanation: Students prefer opportunities to discuss feedback rather than only submitting online surveys, especially to understand why changes can or cannot happen.
quote: “it would be potentially better to have short, like 10-minute feedback sessions... so people can actually talk about it, and figure out why this can or can't be implemented.”
subtheme: Dialogue and closing the feedback loop

explanation: Feedback forms can become less user-friendly when they include demographic or personal questions that students perceive as unnecessary or invasive.
quote: “there are some questions that are constructive. and there are some questions that are redundant. and there's some questions that’s like, mind your own business... boundaries please.”

explanation: Students distinguish between demographic questions that support inclusion and those that ask for unnecessary specificity, highlighting the need for transparent rationale.
quote: “the intention behind it is to see, are we being inclusive?... you don't need to know the specificities of who i like... disability is a different question... that can be something that requires accommodation.”
subtheme: Transparency around data purpose and use

explanation: Anonymity is viewed as essential for encouraging wider and more honest participation, especially from students who may be identifiable through disability, nationality, or other traits.
quote: “anonymity i think is a huge one, for making it more open to a wider demographic... if i think i can be identified because i have a specific disability or a specific nationality... i would be much more hesitant to provide feedback.”

explanation: Students emphasise that feedback mechanisms should be accessible by default, including compatibility with assistive technologies.
quote: “making sure that text to speech and things like that in formatting is accessible... just make it so it's visible. so accessibility as a concept is seen as standard.”

explanation: Students describe informal complaint spaces as emotionally charged and not conducive to effective change because they lack constructive, usable feedback.
quote: “it was kind of like really annoying, not helpful... they go to like the people who are running the course with the attitude of like, we hate you.”

explanation: The programme provided information about how many students responded, helping students evaluate how representative the feedback was.
quote: “we got like a stat on it. it was like ‘how many people responded, what's the standard deviation is’ and everything.”

code: Feedback needs time to resolve issues
explanation: Students note that some issues may resolve over time, but quick implementation still helps because the programme is short and intense.
quote: “some of the issues are being addressed over time... the faculty immediately implemented some changes helped a lot as well.”

explanation: Students felt the delay in electing student representatives was significant because it postponed structured feedback in a short programme.
quote: “the student rep thing happened only a month into the course. so we didn't have any student reps till then.”

explanation: Students identify fear about anonymity as a barrier to honest feedback, especially when feedback goes to someone with authority over them.
quote: “you know, it's anonymous, you're still kind of freaked out... they're even more freaked out about that with like an actual course organizer, like receiving it.”

explanation: Students suggest that offering only one feedback method excludes people with different preferences or comfort levels.
quote: “if people may live a ton of different types of ways that feedback could be given, then, maybe there'd be something for everyone. but it's really only one way to give feedback right now.”

explanation: Students may not engage when they believe nothing actionable will result from their feedback.
quote: “there will be people... they're just gonna be like... nothing's really going to be actionable from here. so why bother giving it.”
subtheme: Belief that feedback leads to change

explanation: Students on a one-year course may feel feedback has limited value if changes will happen only after they leave.
quote: “we are in here for just one year. so by the time they want to implement things we will already be graduate. and what's the point of giving the feedback is it's not going to affect me as an individual.”

explanation: The course’s planned feedback points across the semester create an ongoing cycle rather than a one-off survey.
quote: “we will have an end of semester one too... next semester. so they have like a whole plan set out which is really awesome.”

explanation: Students value being able to send feedback when issues arise, not only at scheduled survey points.
quote: “there's also a forum where you can like send anything at anytime.”

explanation: Students reported that after submitting course feedback they do not receive a response explaining what was heard or what will be changed, reducing trust that feedback has any impact.
quote: primary moderator: "whenever you give out feedback, do you receive any responses from business school?" s2: "no."

explanation: Students want clear confirmation that their feedback has been read and considered, rather than feeling that surveys disappear without visible effect.
quote: s2: "i think it is important to know that the voices of the students are being heard and you’re not just filling our review for..."

explanation: A one-year student felt feedback should lead to changes that benefit the current cohort, not only future students, highlighting the importance of acting while improvements are still useful.
quote: s1: "whatever feedback that i give could be implemented right away... what they keep telling us that whatever feedback you're giving will be applied to the next year's class... how is it gonna do any good to me?"

explanation: Students valued the idea of separating feedback responses into immediate changes and longer-term improvements, so that some action happens quickly where possible.
quote: s1: "i really like what you just said, like the short term and long term, why not? if some things can be implemented now, why not?"

explanation: Students described a cycle where each cohort gives feedback that only improves the next year, limiting the value of feedback as an ongoing improvement process for the current learners.
quote: s1: "my alumni... said the same thing... whatever we are giving now will be better for the next year. but why not this year?"
subtheme: Breaking the cycle of delayed change

explanation: Students said they would be more willing to complete feedback surveys if they saw that prior feedback produced actual change.
quote: s1: "if they did implement some change, i would be like 90%... more willing to do the surveys."

explanation: Students felt that receiving a response such as 'we heard you' would make the process feel worthwhile and meaningful.
quote: s2: "if you were to fill in the survey, and then get feedback, like, ‘okay, we heard you’ makes you feel like, okay, ‘i did it and it is worth it’."

explanation: Without visible outcomes, students questioned the value of continuing to provide feedback through surveys.
quote: s2: "filling surveys are not getting feedback or not seeing the change makes you feel like, why am i even doing this?"

explanation: An example from another group showed feedback being gathered quickly through a poll and acted on within hours by extending a deadline.
quote: primary moderator: "many people are struggling with the course... voted for ‘yes’. and then the lecturer, after just under a couple of hours extended the deadline"

code: Online discussion questions can be misinterpreted
explanation: Students described discussion boards as potentially unclear because questions may be poorly formulated or misunderstood, leading to feedback or answers that do not address the real issue.
quote: s2: "it can be misinterpreted... the lecture was not addressing the exact question. or the question was not formulated in a way to get the proper response."

code: Feedback-led changes to format and content detail
explanation: Student gives examples of collective feedback leading to changes such as more in-person teaching or more detailed topic coverage, indicating effective feedback informs concrete improvements.
quote: “Usually, wanting more things to be in person than online. or wanting certain topics to be covered in more detail.”
subtheme: Concrete changes to teaching delivery and content

code: Course organiser usually best placed to respond
explanation: Student suggests feedback should go to the person with enough contextual understanding to act on it, but escalate when that person does not respond.
quote: “most of the time, the instructor or the course organiser has the most context to actually respond to it. it's only when they don't really want to respond to it, that it makes sense to have it go to someone above them.”
subtheme: Directed to staff with responsibility and contextual knowledge

code: Peer visibility can show how widespread an issue is
explanation: Student proposes allowing classmates to view and support feedback so staff can understand whether a concern is shared, making feedback evidence more tangible.
quote: “allow other students to read feedback the students are writing. so that if the students also agree... they can kind of support it or like it so that the professor knows... how widespread a certain issue is.”

code: In-person interaction makes informal feedback easier
explanation: During the pandemic, feedback became harder because students could not speak to lecturers after class and had to use more formal systems; timely informal routes were reduced.
quote: “during, it was definitely a lot harder to give feedback. because you can’t just like go up after a lecture. you had to go through a more formal route.”

explanation: Student’s ideal system involves small weekly or fortnightly feedback cycles, showing preference for ongoing feedback rather than isolated surveys.
quote: “have more constant feedback. a smaller, like, weekly, or even once every two weeks feedback loop.”

explanation: Student proposes that staff should be required to review feedback results and explain how they plan to address concerns, making feedback transparent and actionable.
quote: “a mandatory acknowledging period by the professors where they go through the results of the feedback after our feedback and kind of outline their plan to address the concerns of their students.”
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop through visible response plans

code: Consistent universal system with visibility and anonymity options
explanation: Student’s ideal feedback system is consistent across all courses and offers options around anonymity and visibility to classmates and course organisers.
quote: “a consistent system that was used for all courses. and that they had the option for anonymity or not, and that your classmates and your course organisers see... what you are posting.”
subtheme: Standardised platform with flexible privacy and visibility

explanation: Students wanted to communicate gaps in teaching or confidence before assessment, allowing staff to adjust support or assessment expectations in time.
quote: "it maybe quite a good way to have some way of feeding back before exams, especially for things that you're worried about... if you don't think that you've been taught the information well enough"

explanation: Students felt demotivated when their feedback could only protect future cohorts while leaving current students disadvantaged by unresolved problems.
quote: "whatever damage was done last semester is done for the exam... all the feedback you're giving us to save the past. but if you're screwed currently, you're still gonna fail"
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop for current students

explanation: The year group chat and student representatives functioned as an ongoing mechanism for gathering issues and escalating common concerns.
quote: "we have like a year group chat... everyone sort of airs out their dirty laundry in there. but the student reps can like take the main point... and then take them to higher up."

code: Need repeated opportunities to fix issues during semester
explanation: Students noted that if they did not feel able to speak during courses, problems accumulated until formal meetings, reducing the chance of timely adjustment.
quote: "everything would pile up to those meetings, which only happened one semester rather than getting fixed, when it could have gotten fixed."
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop for current students

code: Feedback should be routed to responsible actors
explanation: Effective feedback was understood as needing a process where comments are sorted and directed to the staff or units able to respond.
quote: "having someone who can like take in all the feedback, and then decide which group each bit concerned and make sure that everyone who is involved is informed of the feedback."

explanation: Students described feedback as more useful when broad comments were broken down by course area and solutions were developed by the relevant teaching teams.
quote: "they’ll split it up into the individual courses... individually in the course, they found solutions. and then it came back to the course organizer"

explanation: Students linked effective feedback to actual practical changes, such as improved bus services, rather than discussion without implementation.
quote: "there has been progress in terms of changes, which was quite nice, which is something i've never seen happen in the last few years."

explanation: When staff immediately dismissed student concerns about lecture quality, students experienced the feedback process as invalidating and discouraging.
quote: "the feedback we were giving was very, like, dismissive. it was... very disheartening"

code: Need moderated response to sensitive feedback
explanation: Students suggested that feedback should be mediated rather than answered defensively in the moment, so concerns can be considered fairly and constructively.
quote: "maybe having... some sort of moderator to like, take in the responses, decide whether or not they're valid"

code: Exam should reflect taught course content
explanation: Students judged assessment feedback and exam design against whether the exam aligned with what had been taught and what mattered for becoming competent vets.
quote: "a lot of people said that they didn't feel like the course content was reflected in that exam. that exam did not make us either feel like we were better vets or worse vets."
subtheme: Alignment with teaching and professional outcomes

explanation: Feedback mechanisms are described as burdensome and poorly designed when there are too many long, open-ended surveys, reducing student engagement.
quote: “there are too many surveys... the surveys are open ended questions... a big box with a lot of questions. and most of the students will just give it when they look at it”

explanation: A more personal and conversational feedback approach is seen as more accessible and democratic than impersonal surveys alone.
quote: “a more personalized approach is nice... regularly asking for feedback, regularly opening up a conversation... makes it feel more democratic and more accessible”

explanation: Digitised and impersonal feedback systems can exclude or discourage students, especially those who feel marginalised or less comfortable using email-based mechanisms.
quote: “so much feedback is digitized... marginalised students might feel more uncomfortable... if it's so digitized and so impersonal”

explanation: Smaller classes are associated with better feedback experiences because lecturers can manage issues personally and offer extra help.
quote: “most positive ones within a smaller class usually... the lecturer... managed the situation quite well. and they said, they can provide extra help”

explanation: Students suggest tutors could make feedback more accessible in large courses by creating safer discussion spaces and passing concerns to lecturers.
quote: “the tutors can be trained or encouraged to create that environment of a safer space... personalized educational experience, where you feel like you’re seen as an individual enough to like give feedback”

explanation: Students report inconsistent tutorial quality, with some tutors able to explain and support learning well while others simply read standard answers.
quote: “some of the tutors don't know what they're doing... they just read the standard answer... but some tutors are really good... the quality of the tutors, varies”

explanation: Students point to inconsistent or absent standard supports for exams, such as formula booklets, suggesting criteria and expectations are not reliably shared.
quote: “we hadn't ever seriously considered... standardized formula booklets for economic students... that's like something that students have consistently complained about”

explanation: Students call for feedback to be reviewed beyond the individual course organiser to create accountability and reduce subjective dismissal.
quote: “there's some sort of accountability mechanisms, that not just the course organizer that gets the feedback... there's some external bodies... involved in responding to the feedback collection”
subtheme: Accountability and oversight in feedback processes

explanation: Effective feedback is defined as demonstrating that student input is valued and used to improve learning experiences.
quote: “an effective one can show like how students are respected, like the school values our input and try to make the next cohort better”

explanation: Students describe receiving very limited comments on substantial assessments, which does not provide enough concrete information to improve.
quote: “it was like a sentence per question... 40 pages... and then we got like eight sentences, of feedback”

explanation: The participant frames effective feedback as a mechanism for improving courses and supporting student academic performance, rather than as an end in itself.
quote: “the purpose is obviously to make the course better… so it benefits the students too, in order to for them to do well in their academic career.”

explanation: Feedback is seen as more valuable when it produces improvements for later cohorts, though its value for current students depends on whether changes are made quickly.
quote: “I think I find it much more helpful for future students, not so much current student, unless the improvement is done fast.”

explanation: The participant defines effective student feedback by whether it leads to some form of improvement or potential improvement.
quote: “student feedback is effective if an improvement has been made, not necessarily quickly, but if there is, a chance of improvement, therefore it is effective for me.”

explanation: Students may be more willing to provide feedback when they can see that previous feedback has been acted upon, making the feedback process more transparent and credible.
quote: “Yeah, definitely. That would make students want to do it. Because I feel a lot of students don't see change.”

explanation: The participant reports not yet seeing feedback implemented, suggesting a gap between giving feedback and observing its impact.
quote: Moderator: “have you seen any, like feedback actually being implemented?” Participant: “I don't think, no, not yet.”

explanation: The participant expects feedback to be reviewed and translated into an action plan where feasible, while recognising that some changes take longer.
quote: “if they can improve it, then they will improve the feedback immediately, and have an action plan. But I think some things they can't necessarily do or it will take a long process for them to do.”

explanation: Too many feedback requests make the process burdensome, leading the participant to selectively complete only some surveys.
quote: “I do get bombarded with surveys. So I just pick and choose what I think… I will be a good candidate for.”

explanation: Time pressure and competing commitments, including part-time work, are described as barriers to completing feedback surveys.
quote: “probably timewise, because I also do have a part time job… there’s too much feedback, or sorry, too many surveys to do… it’s just like, time consuming.”

explanation: In-person feedback opportunities can be less accessible for commuting students because of travel time and difficulty reaching campus.
quote: “having an in person one again, that's also time consuming. And then it's hard to get to the building sometimes, especially when you commute.”
subtheme: Accessible formats for diverse student circumstances

explanation: The participant suggests paper feedback forms may be easier for students to notice and complete than online surveys, which can get lost in email inboxes.
quote: “I think… paper surveys… they’re more willing to do it if it's a paper form… Online… sometimes you just get lost with all your emails, you've just missed the survey.”

code: Anonymity increases willingness to give feedback
explanation: Students report that lack of anonymity on Piazza discourages them from giving feedback, especially when names are identifiable to course organisers.
quote: "you can have the option of being anonymous to all the other students... they can still see your name, like the course organizers. and i know that that's definitely put me off"

code: Feedback results shared back to students
explanation: In a small class, lecturers discussed feedback findings with students and addressed main points, making the feedback process visible.
quote: "the following week... she like discussed pretty much the results from the lecture and also from feedback as well... they showed they had taken that into account"

explanation: The student contrasts small classes where most people are heard with large courses where only some topics or groups seem to receive attention.
quote: "in a lot of our larger courses, it feels less like... we're all being heard... it feels like they're only focusing on certain courses, or certain like groups of people"

explanation: The student stresses that feedback is most effective when changes are implemented while they are still taking the course, so they can benefit from it.
quote: "what makes feedback more effective is if you can actually see it being like the results were being implemented, whilst you're still learning or taking that course"

code: Delayed improvements feel useless to current students
explanation: When changes only help the next cohort, students feel their feedback has limited value because they cannot use the improvement themselves.
quote: "in so many cases, it’s not until the following year. so it kind of feels a bit useless... it would be nice if things could help us now"

code: Earlier release of materials helps preparation
explanation: Students gave feedback requesting pre-recorded videos be uploaded earlier, and this concrete change gave them more time to prepare.
quote: "instead of uploading the videos on thursdays, we'll put it on tuesdays. and that happened, during, whilst we were taking the course"

code: Sample paper did not match exam difficulty
explanation: The student describes feedback asking for more exam preparation materials because the available sample paper did not provide a clear guide to the assessment goal.
quote: "can you at least give us one or two more? like, so we have a better idea of this exam?... the exam was way harder than sample paper"

explanation: Students want feedback to be read by those with authority to make relevant changes, such as course organisers or heads of school.
quote: "basically whoever has the most influence to change things based on what they've gotten... sometimes... i'm not always sure if it like gets to the right people"
subtheme: Reaching people with power to act

explanation: The student suggests feedback should be more frequent than mid-semester and end-of-semester forms, enabling a more continuous improvement process.
quote: "make it more frequent, to be able to give feedback... not just like once or twice a semester"

explanation: Students worry that identifiable feedback could lead to judgement or consequences, reducing their willingness to be honest.
quote: "i don't want to... be like, they will know that this is me. so there could be some consequences to me being the one... i'd prefer for me to remain anonymous"

explanation: The participant sees the rating-scale forms as acceptable for collecting opinions, but feels the process lacks transparency because students are not shown whether or how their responses are used.
quote: “they're quite good with the whole... agree, disagree. and you're given an option to further explain. i just don't know how much that is put into use”

explanation: The participant suggests face-to-face feedback collection may be more effective and inclusive because many students ignore email forms.
quote: “maybe collecting feedback from people in person might be more useful... i'm probably in the minority for filling them out often”

explanation: The participant proposes using small-group teaching spaces at the end of a course to invite student feedback, making the process easier to participate in.
quote: “maybe in the last tutorial, it would be a good idea. at the end... just ask if anyone has any feedback”

explanation: The participant gives feedback because they want the university experience to improve, partly because they and their family invest significant money in it.
quote: “it's just wanting to see things get better here. since i do spend a lot of time here, and my parents have spent a lot of money sending me”

explanation: The participant reports not seeing their feedback lead to identifiable changes, weakening confidence in the process.
quote: “Have you ever seen visibly sort of feedback get implemented after you've given it? ... not really. no.”

explanation: The participant wants the university to report back on what feedback has been received and what action is being taken, making the impact of student feedback observable.
quote: “it would be nice to see that for sure... they never really send out anything about it being implemented”

explanation: Receiving a direct response from staff, even when the issue cannot be resolved, is valued more than submitting feedback into an online system with no reply.
quote: “yeah, because i got a response in a way even though... my worries weren't calmed, it was still better to get some type of response than nothing”

explanation: The participant feels there are too many repeated surveys asking the same questions, which reduces engagement and makes feedback feel performative rather than useful.
quote: “i feel like i received several in a semester... i'm continuously being asked to give feedback, exact same things”

explanation: The participant does not know who receives or processes submitted feedback, indicating a lack of transparency in the feedback system.
quote: “what do you think happens to your when you fill that... no, i don't know. because maybe like, student association or something like that”

explanation: The participant recognises email forms are broadly accessible, but the process may still discourage engagement because it feels impersonal and disconnected.
quote: “the email forms, i guess everyone can get a hold of... it feels quite impersonal in a way”

code: Feedback barrier through being passed around
explanation: When seeking an answer, the participant experienced emails being redirected between staff, creating a practical barrier and delaying resolution.
quote: “my email was just kind of being passed around with everyone saying like, oh, we don't really know, ask this person... in the end, i was in contact with the principal”

explanation: The participant describes delays of weeks before reaching the right person, making feedback or requests less useful because responses are not prompt.
quote: “no one really knows who to contact within the eca... sometimes it takes a good couple of weeks until you get to who you want to get a hold of”

explanation: The participant was told before enrolment that a business/history of art combination would be possible, then later told it was impossible, showing unreliable communication and undermining trust.
quote: “they said, yes, that's for sure... and then i got here... i was told that business was impossible to do with history of art”

code: Communication between university parts needs improvement
explanation: The participant identifies poor communication between different parts of the university as a problem affecting students' ability to act on information.
quote: “there needs to be communication between students, and... the different parts of the university”

explanation: The participant does not see meaningful communication between staff and students about how collected feedback is used after submission.
quote: “in terms of giving feedback... how that feedback is used afterwards?... no, i don't really think so. at least it's not what i've seen”

code: Effective feedback requires evidence of action
explanation: The participant defines effective student feedback as seeing efforts being made and receiving a summary of what the university is doing in response.
quote: “at least, to see some efforts being made... getting a rundown of what feedback has been given to the university and what they are currently doing to implement it”

explanation: The participant feels frequent repeated requests make feedback seem like a symbolic exercise rather than a meaningful process for change.
quote: “most people will start to disregard it... it seems like it's almost become just like a show to send it out... so that people think they're being heard”

code: Feedback should lead to concrete options
explanation: In response to pandemic learning concerns, the participant wanted the university to explore practical alternatives, such as more engaging delivery and more study spaces.
quote: “just maybe look at other options, look at ways to make it more engaging... even just spaces for people to be on their computers”

explanation: The participant favours combining online and in-person methods so students with different time constraints and preferences can still give feedback.
quote: “i definitely think a mixture of both, because some people will not have the time... to get somewhere physically to give feedback”

code: Lack of visible outcomes discourages future feedback
explanation: Because the participant repeatedly gives similar feedback without seeing change, the process starts to feel pointless and discourages continued participation.
quote: “i'm filling out the form with the same things every single time... it just seems futile. at this point”

explanation: The student describes lengthy feedback forms as boring and effortful, suggesting that feedback mechanisms need to be easy to use and not overly burdensome for students.
quote: "sometimes, like the feedback process can just be really boring. like, if the form is like this really long form. there's like loads and loads of questions... i wish it was just every feedback form, like you could save your progress"

explanation: Students want visible acknowledgement that their feedback has been received, even where changes cannot be made. This reflects a need for transparent communication about what happens after feedback is submitted.
quote: "you through all the effort to put all your stuff down and send it and then nothing happens... even if, like, they don't implement anything, sometimes all you want is at least like, like an acknowledgement"

code: Feedback should lead to visible action
explanation: A core marker of effective feedback is that it is translated into concrete changes rather than simply collected repeatedly.
quote: "it's easy to just keep on asking for feedback after feedback... but what are the actions been taken after that? and how is my feedback being incorporated into like strategy"

explanation: The student reports confusion because coursework instructions and follow-up information were unclear, indicating a need for feedback and guidance that is understandable and transparent to learners.
quote: "we were just very confused the whole time, because the initial instructions for the course were like, didn't make any sense... follow up information and lectures and stuff, which is very strange and unclear"

explanation: Students felt that course information was released too close to deadlines, limiting their ability to use it effectively.
quote: "they don't always tell us everything until closer to the last minute"

explanation: The student describes submitting issues through class reps but seeing little evidence that these were recorded or discussed, undermining transparency in the feedback loop.
quote: "they always post their minutes for the meeting... and yeah, it didn’t seem like it was really going anywhere. because it didn't come up in the minutes of the meeting"

explanation: Even when student concerns are discussed, the resulting action points are perceived as insufficient compared with the issues raised.
quote: "even if what i've said does pop up... it almost never covers like action for everything... the actions like pales in comparison to what was actually discussed"

explanation: A student identifies an instance where feedback about lack of support during strikes led to a changed deadline, showing feedback becoming concretely actionable.
quote: "we raised that issue... i think they like extended the deadline or like release date for like the next one or something. so i guess that one did work"

explanation: The student views feedback processes as effective when lecturers respond quickly and make amendments based on student input.
quote: "the lecturers are just quick to respond to and make amendments to whatever... they've acted on that. so i think they're working"

explanation: Having both in-class and form-based options lets students choose the mode that suits their comfort level, supporting a more usable feedback system.
quote: "they had a form that we could fill in... they also asked for feedback in the lecture... at least having those options because some people do feel more comfortable like just saying things directly"

explanation: The participant argues feedback may be more effective at the end of semester because midterm requests occur when students are busy with deadlines and still adapting.
quote: “keeping the feedback to the end of the semester, that would be a good idea… I don't think I did any of them in time to mid term feedback, because I had so many deadlines.”
subtheme: Appropriate point in the learning journey

explanation: The participant feels midterm feedback can come before students have enough experience of the course to provide meaningful comments.
quote: “even with the midterm feedback, sometimes you're still adapting to university life. Like, I feel like it comes too soon… what do I have to give feedback on? I feel like I've just started the semester.”
subtheme: Appropriate point in the learning journey

explanation: The participant supports a cyclical process where feedback is gathered, reviewed, and used to make changes for the following semester or year.
quote: Moderator: “they get back to you… saying, this is what we're gonna do for the courses for the second semester…” Participant: “Yeah, I think that's a better idea.”
subtheme: Closing the feedback loop across semesters

explanation: Asking students why something is not working and how it could be improved is seen as a way to move feedback beyond complaints into constructive suggestions.
quote: “I feel like asking them why, like, how they can improve, that's probably a good way… I always asked, what don't you like, and how, how or why we can improve it.”

explanation: The participant gives an example of useful feedback that identifies a specific class issue and proposes a concrete change to who should attend it.
quote: “some students did give suggestions… they didn't think that it was worth going, because it was just a repeat on first year. So they said, maybe just have it for direct entry second year students instead of the whole… second year.”

explanation: The participant suggests students often prefer quick yes/no style feedback rather than long written responses, indicating that feedback mechanisms should not be overly demanding.
quote: “I just want to quickly ‘yes’ or ‘no’. Yes, I get it from a student perspective. They don't want to do it.”

explanation: The participant recognises that feedback can reveal conflicting student needs, requiring the university to balance different preferences when making improvements.
quote: “some people prefer to online and some people didn't. So I guess it's like, you need to balance both sides.”

explanation: The participant sees anonymity as important because some students may be reluctant to share opinions if they feel personally identifiable.
quote: “I think that is important because some students are a bit shy to give their opinion… they don't want their name to be on the feedback form.”

explanation: Voucher incentives are described as a motivator for completing surveys and attending feedback sessions, though this relates more to participation than feedback quality.
quote: “because of the voucher. That did motivate me, if I'm being honest.”

explanation: The participant believes students who are more involved in university life are more likely to provide feedback, while less connected students may participate less.
quote: Moderator: “do you think that more involved students give feedback more?” Participant: “Yeah, definitely. So it's just kind of up to the student.”

explanation: Student describes feedback being requested too late to benefit the students who provided it, limiting its usefulness because changes are deferred to future cohorts.
quote: “it often felt like it was asked too late for the feedback to be implemented... ‘for the next cohort’ like, okay, what about my cohort?”
subtheme: Feedback in time to benefit current students

explanation: Midterm feedback is perceived as ineffective when it cannot influence the current semester, reducing the value of collecting it at that point.
quote: “the midterm one is not very useful, because they won't change it anyway. so why they're doing that?”
subtheme: Feedback in time to benefit current students

explanation: Positive feedback practice is associated with lecturers repeatedly inviting feedback and reassuring students that it will be applied where possible.
quote: “she very consistently was like asking for feedback... up until the very end, she was like, send me feedback. and i'll apply it if i can”

explanation: Student notes that good course experiences often arise where lecturers have already incorporated feedback from earlier cohorts, showing feedback as part of an improvement cycle.
quote: “the lecturers have taken feedback from previous cohorts and applied them”

explanation: Student argues effective feedback requires an ongoing space throughout the course so concerns can be addressed as they happen rather than only at the end.
quote: “having avenues for consistent feedback, maybe even like every week... a space for feedback that's present from week one to the end of the course to address students concerns as they are happening in real time”

explanation: Lecturer response is experienced as defensive and dismissive rather than using criticism to identify improvements, undermining actionability.
quote: “basically, like defended it all, every single... criticism that was made... just ignored the negative feedback”

explanation: Students find vague institutional responses unhelpful because they do not specify what will change, when, or why action cannot be taken.
quote: “‘okay, we will take this into account, but it will not happen this semester’... the phrase like ‘take this into account’ makes me feel very annoying. because what does it mean?”

explanation: Students report not knowing how survey data are used or whether it affects teaching, indicating a lack of transparent feedback processing.
quote: “there is a problem and often like there's no transparency in terms of how that information is being used. unless the lecturer chooses to discuss it”

explanation: Student proposes sharing meeting minutes and outcomes so students can see how feedback is treated and acted upon.
quote: “having those minutes, like parts of the minutes shared with the student body so that we know what's going on in those meetings”

explanation: Students want clearer access to basic course data, such as class size, because lack of transparency contributes to an impersonal experience.
quote: “can those data be... more transparent, because they will tell us like how many people are in this class?... for all the courses, like everything is so... it's not transparent”

explanation: Students valued feedback when the University summarised the main issues raised and explicitly reported what changes would be made, creating a sense that their input had consequences.
quote: "they marked out the major ones. and they did come and tell us about it. and they told us the changes that were happening because of it. and i thought that was really nice"

explanation: Seeing the effects of feedback made the process feel meaningful and increased students’ sense of agency in change.
quote: "because it makes you feel like you're fixing things. i am a part of the change because i can see it."

explanation: Survey questions written by students were perceived as more useful because they targeted issues that mattered to the cohort rather than reflecting only staff assumptions.
quote: "they made questions, which was really useful rather than professors making questions"

explanation: Students described QR-code feedback in lectures as easier to complete than email surveys, especially when brief and embedded into existing sessions.
quote: "that's why i think the qr codes work a lot better... purely because i don't respond to single surveys"

explanation: Students reported that email is an ineffective feedback communication channel because of volume and low engagement, meaning requests or outcomes can be missed.
quote: "email's not a good way of communicating with us. just because we get so many of them, there's just no point."

explanation: The volume of unrelated survey requests led students to ignore surveys, including potentially important University feedback opportunities.
quote: "we just get like so many surveys... when someone does try and send a survey around for something like uni related, i mean, i personally i just don’t have a look at it."

code: Feedback after exams is too late
explanation: Students felt that feedback gathered only after exams could not help those currently affected by poor teaching or assessment design.
quote: "we have the feedback after exams... it wasn't until after the exam and the feedback session that suddenly they were made aware of how everyone was just like, terrified."

explanation: Students identified that feedback may eventually lead to change, but delays are damaging when the issue affects current learning and assessment.
quote: "it just takes a while for the change to happen when realistically, when it's related to the course, the level of education should be a lot quicker."

explanation: Non-academic feedback/support responses were experienced as ineffective when they arrived after the student had already resolved the problem.
quote: "i've tried emailing sometimes, and it takes forever to get back to me... it just took a week and a half. and by the time i had already fixed it. i was like this was no longer helpful."

code: Need anticipatory feedback before problems escalate
explanation: Students wanted mechanisms to raise concerns before exams or before issues became serious, so the University could intervene while there was still time to act.
quote: "i wonder if there’s a way to have feedback like, before it's a problem."

code: Limited lecturer control over feedback channels
explanation: Students perceived that lecturers may not directly manage Learn pages or uploaded materials, which can obscure who receives issues and who can act on them.
quote: s1: "the professor doesn't deal with the learn directly... the professor has nothing to do with like, except from posting those sessions"

explanation: Students explicitly defined useful feedback processes as those where changes are implemented promptly enough for the current student group to benefit.
quote: s2: "i think implementing the changes straightaway is really useful... giving the feedback now for the next year is not... you don't benefit enough, as a current student."

explanation: Students noted that feedback gathered in lectures or tutorials may overrepresent attendees or confident speakers and miss absent or shy students.
quote: s2: "one, you have students that don't attend, two, you have students that attend and are okay with the content. and three, you have students that are too shy. so, i don't know..."

explanation: A student suggested that those actively attending understand course problems better and may provide more meaningful feedback than those who complete surveys carelessly.
quote: s1: "students who are not attending won't know how bad the structure is... the ones who are actually attending... might fill in more constructively"
subtheme: Quality and representativeness of student voice

explanation: Long surveys reduce engagement; students prefer shorter formats that still allow them to communicate key issues.
quote: s1: "if it's too long, then i do not want to... a short survey, but also be able to get my point across."

explanation: Seeing progress through a survey makes the feedback process more manageable and encourages completion.
quote: s1: "if i do not see the bar... to tell me how much i’ve progressed through the survey... ‘how long is it gonna take?’"

explanation: Students may quit surveys when they are forced to answer too many questions, showing the importance of accessible feedback mechanisms.
quote: primary moderator: "you have to answer all the questions... i just quit the survey." s2: "yes."

explanation: Even when students have time to complete feedback, uncertainty about whether it will lead to change reduces motivation.
quote: s2: "even if you had the time would things change?"

explanation: Asking students to complete feedback immediately during or after events may produce rushed, less thoughtful responses because of social and environmental distractions.
quote: s1: "they put the qr on the projector... there's a lot of stuffs happening around... you do not really fill in with full dedication"
subtheme: Appropriate timing and context for feedback

explanation: QR-based feedback can be impractical if students scan the code but later lose the tab, preventing them from submitting feedback.
quote: s2: "i scan the qr code, put my phone away, and then i close all the tabs. and it's gone. so i'm not able to provide feedback."

explanation: Students value knowing what happens after feedback is submitted; without visible follow-up, surveys feel disconnected from outcomes.
quote: “i like talking to like the different program reps... or like, i'm not really sure what happened after that. so i just don't know.”

explanation: Feedback mechanisms can become burdensome when they rely on lengthy or repetitive surveys, reducing willingness to respond.
quote: “i find feedback surveys to be a little tedious in the process and filling out all of that.”

explanation: The student suggests feedback should be easy to provide at the moment an issue occurs, before thoughts are lost.
quote: “if it could be like, as soon as you feel like something's not right, you just put that down, that will be great.”

explanation: Students feel unsure about who has authority to receive or act on feedback beyond the programme level.
quote: “i don't know what till what level the authority goes in university here... i don't know how it works in edinburgh university.”
