explanation: Students want feedback processes to demonstrate reciprocal communication and meaningful outcomes, rather than only collecting opinions.
quote: “is it really is the communication in two ways?... i will give all my time and energy to give this feedback, but what is really going to come back to me, so it's a bit what is the point?”

explanation: Students were impressed when the programme summarised feedback and explained short- and long-term responses, making the feedback process visible.
quote: “they kind of gave a summary of like, the good points... the bad points. and then they were like, here's what we're going to do in the short term, here's what we're going to do in the long term.”

explanation: Students perceived feedback as effective because staff acted quickly on identified issues.
quote: “they actually have already done theirs... actually, they have really done the short term. that really impressed me.”

explanation: Feedback about wanting more lecturer contact led to a rapid response from the course team.
quote: “so we gave that feedback. and like, the response was immediate. and now the senior teaching fellows...”

explanation: Students contrast their course’s responsiveness with wider university surveys where they cannot tell whether feedback leads anywhere.
quote: “they did that survey too... we have no way of knowing if that stuff is actually... which is my usual experience.”

explanation: Students are motivated to provide feedback when they believe it can lead to concrete changes.
quote: “we really wanted to get something like we wanted some sort of change... that could be a means to actually doing something about it.”

explanation: Students want to know whether their feedback leads to change; without visible implementation, the feedback process feels inefficient and uncertain.
quote: “how do we know that feedback is, like, implemented into something? yeah, how to make the whole process as efficient as possible.”

explanation: A liaison meeting was experienced as productive but poorly organised, reducing clarity about how feedback is handled and who is responsible for the process.
quote: “it was productive. but it also seemed a bit disorganized... the person who organized the meeting wasn't there... nobody really had any idea for the first 15 minutes.”

explanation: Students valued staff who were present, interested, and allowed students sufficient space to share their views.
quote: “the professors who showed up to the meeting were very interested in what we had to say. and they gave us all the space to say the things that we wanted to.”

explanation: Students may avoid giving honest feedback when the person being discussed is present or in a position of authority over them.
quote: “we don't always feel comfortable bringing that up, since that person is, number one, present in the meetings. and number two... this is like our course organizer.”

explanation: Computer-based surveys are perceived as boring and easy to disengage from, even when students have meaningful feedback to give.
quote: “it's always, for me, on the computer, like surveys. and they're just a bit boring. and i have a lot of input i want to give... and then i just get to the laptop and say, nah, whatever, i can’t be bothered.”

explanation: When the same feedback is raised repeatedly but receives only dismissive responses, students perceive the feedback process as lacking meaningful follow-through.
quote: “feedback had been repeated in about six staff-student liaison committee meetings... exactly the same feedback... and the response was, oh, yeah... ‘this is how we do it’ is not an answer.”

explanation: Students accept that feedback cannot always be acted upon, but want clear explanations when the answer is no.
quote: “sometimes we ask, and the answer is no, but tell us why. because ‘just because it's how we do it’ isn't an answer. there's usually a reason for it.”

explanation: Closed survey questions can restrict students’ ability to explain issues and may produce feedback that flatters staff rather than captures actionable concerns.
quote: “you'll have discrepancies between only providing closed questions... i can very, very nicely procure closed question feedback, that wouldn't really give my students space to elaborate and actually provide elaborate feedback.”

code: Generic surveys inadequate for experimental courses
explanation: For a new or experimental course, standard end-of-course surveys are seen as insufficiently responsive to the need for detailed, course-specific feedback.
quote: “for an experimental course... they should probably have better feedback requests than just the standard survey that they get everyone else.”

explanation: Students generate feedback throughout a course, but being asked only at survey time makes it harder to recall and communicate all relevant points.
quote: “you come up with feedback throughout the course. and then you're just given the survey... i have so much more to say than i could say.”

code: Mid-course feedback can enable within-course changes
explanation: Student describes mid-course feedback leading to an actionable change in teaching format, suggesting feedback is useful when it can alter practice before the course ends.
quote: “one of our courses only had online classes, and asynchronous videos to watch, and a lot of feedback from the class was given to like, make it live and have live sessions, in addition to the asynchronous lectures.”
subtheme: Responsive changes to current teaching practice

code: Feedback timing halfway through semester may be too late
explanation: Student argues that feedback collected halfway through a course can miss the window for meaningful change, and proposes earlier collection while there is still time to respond.
quote: “if you're giving feedback for it halfway through the semester, it's like kind of almost too late to do anything about it. like it might be better to have one like a quarter of the way into semester, like three or four weeks in”
subtheme: Early enough to influence the current course

explanation: Student suggests shorter, more frequent surveys would be easier to complete and may increase engagement compared with long feedback forms.
quote: “having shorter surveys might be a better idea. because having two long surveys instead of say, a short one at the end of every lecture or something like that, meant that people do not want to respond to it.”

code: Time and effort affect willingness to give feedback
explanation: Feedback processes are seen as less effective when they require too much time or effort, implying that user-friendly feedback systems should be quick and easy to use.
quote: “time is definitely a motivating factor. if it requires too much time and requires too much effort, i would be less willing to give feedback rather than if it was easier to do it.”

code: Perceived lack of change discourages feedback
explanation: Student reports that when courses have a reputation for not improving, giving feedback feels pointless, showing that feedback needs to lead to observable action to maintain trust and engagement.
quote: “everyone knows that it's a badly-run course and that it's not going to change. so there's no point doing any feedback things for it.”

explanation: Students are uncertain about who receives or reads their feedback, indicating a lack of transparency in the feedback process.
quote: “i don't think the questionnaire says where the data’s going? i've always assumed that the quantitative... are somewhat accreted and sent up to someone in the school, but that the individual comments probably only go to the course organiser, but that may be completely wrong.”

code: Sharing feedback results and planned improvements
explanation: Student values lecturers spending class time explaining feedback results and how they will improve, making the feedback process visible and transparent.
quote: “for a certain few of my classes, after we had feedback, we had, like 10 minutes spent on the results of the feedback and how they would do better.”

code: Seeing feedback acted on encourages future feedback
explanation: Observable implementation of feedback motivates students to keep participating, because they can see their input has impact.
quote: “yeah, definitely. i think seeing feedback being brought to action is definitely an encouraging thing.”

explanation: Student distinguishes between one-off problems and long-standing issues that remain despite feedback, indicating the importance of an ongoing improvement cycle rather than isolated feedback collection.
quote: “when there’s some part of a course is bad, they run like once, and then they actually respond to feedback, people are like, ‘whatever, it happens’... but when it's courses that we've had... that's still true.”

code: Feedback systems may overrepresent engaged students
explanation: Students who attend and engage with courses are more likely to provide feedback, while those struggling may be underrepresented; this affects whether feedback reflects the full learner experience.
quote: “it's kind of biased towards people who are already engaging with the course... whereas people who might be really struggling with the course, like, don't have the time or the motivation to fill out feedback forms for it.”

explanation: Students want feedback to reach people with direct responsibility and power to act, such as the course professor, programme representative, and programme director.
quote: s1: "i want my course professor to read it... the second person should be the programme rep... programme director has direct control over how the program's been around."

explanation: Students felt feedback should be escalated when the immediate programme leadership does not act, so issues can still lead to change.
quote: s1: "if i see that my programme director doesn't really do much, or doesn't take any initiative, then... perhaps someone who was the main boss"

explanation: A student described two-week course blocks as too rushed to allow in-depth learning, suggesting feedback should address structural barriers to achieving learning goals.
quote: s1: "just finishing one course in just two weeks... i'm not able to learn any of my courses in depth."
subtheme: Workload and pacing aligned with learning goals

code: Assessment workload misaligned with learning capacity
explanation: Students described heavy assessment demands and rapid deadlines as undermining learning and wellbeing, indicating feedback should connect workload to achievable learning goals.
quote: s1: "after every two weeks, i have an assignment. and i've fallen sick twice because of so much... overload of work"
subtheme: Workload and pacing aligned with learning goals

explanation: A mature student argued that feedback and university responses should consider differing student circumstances, especially parents and carers, rather than applying inflexible decisions.
quote: s2: "they should be a little bit more empathy from the university, that our circumstances are a little bit different... she just requested an extension and she got denied."

explanation: A student wanted coursework demands to be moderated because multiple tasks in one subject felt excessive and time-consuming.
quote: s2: "we had a group presentation... another group to do a homework... now we have to do an atp... it's too much work for one subject"
subtheme: Workload and pacing aligned with learning goals

explanation: A student felt group work should not carry too high a grade weighting because free riders can unfairly affect individual outcomes.
quote: s1: "if you're giving group work, don't make it 50% of your grade. maybe 20-30% is fine."
subtheme: Fair and reliable group assessment processes

explanation: Students were unsure how peer review marks affect grades, making the process feel opaque and difficult to use fairly.
quote: s2: "i'm still trying to work out how it works in here... i got the lowest score. so, i'm wondering how it works."
subtheme: Clarity of assessment mechanisms and consequences

code: Fear of penalty for honest peer feedback
explanation: A student worried that marking non-contributing peers down might be interpreted negatively and penalise the honest evaluator, suggesting inconsistent or unclear criteria.
quote: s2: "if you mark them low, they will say that you cannot work as a team... i could penalise in a way for telling the truth. so, it's a bit of a grey area."
subtheme: Fair and reliable group assessment processes

explanation: The peer marking system was perceived as vulnerable to strategic marking rather than reliable assessment of contribution.
quote: primary moderator: "it's like... is he gonna mark me full marks or is he gonna mark me down? if he's gonna mark me down. i'm gonna mark him down."
subtheme: Fair and reliable group assessment processes

explanation: Online-only feedback may be easy to ignore, while in-person formats may prompt more participation.
quote: “if the lecture is just asked online, not do it... perhaps not face to face, i wouldn't actually do it if i had more concerns.”

explanation: Students want clearer access to decision-makers above the programme when issues cannot be resolved locally.
quote: “having more access to the higher levels of that would be good.”

explanation: Students link effective change to understanding who is responsible for major decisions, such as cohort size.
quote: “if you want to make real changes... reducing the number of people in my program, like, we need to know who was making those decisions.”

explanation: Understanding which staff can control which decisions would help students direct feedback appropriately and maintain relationships.
quote: “understanding that will also help us empathize with the program organizers. i mean, you don't want to go to them... complaining about something that they have no control over.”

explanation: Students describe accommodation issues where feedback or complaints took too long to resolve, reducing effectiveness.
quote: “it doesn't get addressed soon enough. we had like a woman problem. and it persisted for 20 days, because they just said it'll take that long.”

explanation: Although communication around accommodation complaints was supportive, the available actions were not seen as helpful.
quote: “the flow of information and for communication has been great. but it's just that the options themselves aren't very helpful.”

explanation: Students worry that formal complaint processes may expose them and create risks when they must continue living with the person complained about.
quote: “whatever we say to them, like as complaints, will no longer remain anonymous... they will know that it was you who complained, but you still have to live with them.”

explanation: Students identify fatigue from repeated surveys as a reason feedback may fail to capture underrepresented voices.
quote: “there is response fatigue, people are just like, tired of answering surveys... you barely get like 10... things to it.”

explanation: Students worry that those who are less vocal, busier, or struggling may not be heard through standard feedback channels.
quote: “we are a particularly vocal group... there are people out there who are facing very different issues... because they don't speak up normally... you're not going to hear their feedback and they're going to suffer alone.”

explanation: Students see face-to-face feedback as more impactful because tone, body language, and personal presence communicate more than written survey responses.
quote: “speaking and being physically present, like, sense body language, sense tone of voice. there's a lot that goes into it. like it's more impactful.”

explanation: Students experience frustration when the person receiving feedback is not empowered to act on it, making the feedback route seem ineffective.
quote: “the person receiving the feedback can't always actually go and provide the feedback in a way that makes them feel comfortable.”

explanation: Students explicitly identify transparency as a key condition for better feedback systems, particularly to avoid vague justifications based on tradition.
quote: “mine doesn't cost money. anonymity, multimodality, and transparency... ‘oh, it's just because we've always done it’.”

explanation: Students want online surveys retained as an option but supplemented by direct conversations with lecturers where appropriate.
quote: “less online surveys... more talking to the people... have the option also, having this online survey... but... being able to talk to the lecturers.”

explanation: Students link transparent feedback processes to a stronger sense of belonging and mutual responsibility within the university community.
quote: “transparency really helps with that, because you kind of see, like, oh, this is why the people above us are doing what they're doing. and hopefully you see that it's for us.”

explanation: Students may be less likely to give feedback if they do not know whether others share their concerns.
quote: “it would potentially stop people from giving feedback, because they don't know other people feel that way... they’re the only ones that think this.”

explanation: Focus-group style feedback can help students feel less alone by hearing others articulate similar experiences.
quote: “giving feedback in this sort of environment... saying things that i thought before but haven't put into words, makes me feel like i’m not just experiencing these things alone.”

explanation: Small mandatory tutorial groups are suggested as a less intimidating and more accessible setting for giving feedback.
quote: “tutorial groups... would perhaps be the best kind of time and place to give feedback... it's a small group, so you don't feel as intimidated... your tutor is usually not like the lecturer.”

explanation: Students propose small course-credit incentives for giving feedback, particularly where similar credit is already offered for research participation.
quote: “i don't see any issue with even 2-5% of the course credits being given to providing feedback. and these are four options by which you can provide feedback.”

explanation: When asked what they would change, the participant prioritises actual implementation of feedback over collection alone.
quote: “what would be the first thing you did... in terms of student feedback?... implementing the feedback”

explanation: A student says anonymity lets them give necessary critical feedback without over-filtering their message, while still remaining polite.
quote: "i want to be able to slightly like not filter what i'm saying... i want to be harsh sometimes... i can do that anonymously"

explanation: Students repeatedly raised an issue about restoring 24-hour access to Appleton Tower, but no action occurred despite frequent feedback.
quote: "practically every other week, like we express this to like, it would be so helpful and everything but yeah, nothing's happened"

explanation: Targeted listening groups are viewed as a useful way to ensure minority or underrepresented students have structured opportunities to be heard.
quote: "listening groups... specific groups of students, for example, female students, international students... making sure that these groups get to be heard"

code: Collated listening group outcomes preserve confidentiality
explanation: Although listening groups are not fully anonymous in the room, collated reporting without attribution helps make outcomes transparent while protecting individuals.
quote: "they like emailed out the results... none of those were like attributed to anybody - it was collated and stuff"

explanation: Embedding feedback forms directly in course pages may make them more visible and easier for students to complete than email-based requests.
quote: “instead of having it on the emails, would have it fit on the course page. so the first thing that you see... is a sort of feedback form, which you can directly kind of fill in.”

explanation: Students report that rewards or useful resources can strongly motivate participation in feedback activities.
quote: “if this didn’t have the voucher, i wouldn't have come... i think that's the only way i can see... something people want.”

explanation: A student received many responses by offering lecture materials in exchange, showing that students are more likely to give feedback when the process has immediate value to them.
quote: “if you want the lecture slides and the recording, qr code... i got 186 responses for that feedback session... they wanted something i was able to provide, but i did request feedback.”

explanation: Students may not provide feedback if they see the university only as a service provider rather than a community they belong to.
quote: “if you see it only as a transactional interaction or space, then you're not going to bother telling them that the lecturer is annoying, or the lectures are too early, or the building is too cold or just not accessible.”

explanation: Students suggest that feedback systems should include representatives from communities less likely to participate through mainstream routes.
quote: “having representatives from these quieter communities is quite important... get people from those communities to represent them into sort of giving feedback.”

explanation: Short, relaxed in-person feedback sessions are seen as a useful complement to surveys, although anonymity remains a concern.
quote: “just a ten-minute chat with lecturer... make sure it's very chill... anonymity then becomes a problem... just a relaxed environment.”

explanation: Paper-based midterm feedback was valued as a simple, timely method for capturing student views during the course rather than only at the end.
quote: “do they still do midterm paper feedback?... we got little papers... you got it at the beginning of the lecture... sorry, i loved that, though.”

explanation: Students advocate offering multiple ways to give feedback rather than relying on a single survey format.
quote: “multimodality... having the meeting, it's not necessarily a replacement for the questionnaires but it could absolutely be a platform... in addition to the papers or questionnaires.”

explanation: Students identify class representatives as a possible route for sensitive feedback to reach staff without exposing the individual student.
quote: “how that feedback would reach him without, you know, a student being a face of the message... an additional way of providing feedback to the class reps, so it's not going directly to the teacher.”

explanation: Fear of negative consequences from staff can inhibit honest feedback, particularly where power differences are significant.
quote: “absolutely. and i was told i should be very careful... by the head of the school.”

explanation: Regular meetings between course representatives and organisers provide a continuing mechanism for concerns to be raised and acted on.
quote: “the course reps meet the course organiser every month... all the concerns are addressed, and then like the course organiser will take it to the meeting.”

explanation: Students see effective feedback as involving decisions about immediate and future actions after issues are raised.
quote: “they decide what to do, what are the long term, short term plans and then they implement.”

explanation: Students appreciate being informed about what staff plan to do, rather than feeling excluded after submitting feedback.
quote: “we will receive an email... what they plan to do. every one is part of the process. it's not just isolating us.”

code: More frequent than once per semester
explanation: Monthly feedback meetings are seen as more appropriate than once-per-semester feedback for a short one-year programme.
quote: “in the past, it's only been once a semester, which is really just not enough... she suggested, okay, let's do this one once a month.”

explanation: Students requested a Q&A session so they could ask concrete questions and receive guidance relevant to their assessment preparation.
quote: “one of the lecturers the idea of arranging a session. and we have it next week... the team actually arranging it.”

explanation: Effective feedback requires demonstrable action, not just collecting survey responses as symbolic evidence of caring.
quote: “actual evidence, not just like, quote, evidence of caring, which is like, okay, we're sending out the survey. so we care, that doesn't really mean that much.”

explanation: Students valued feedback responses that clearly matched each concern with a proposed solution.
quote: “this is the question, this is answer; this is the issue, and this is our solution.”

explanation: A student states anonymity is necessary to obtain accurate feedback and to ensure they would participate.
quote: “it has to be... because if it's not, it's really not going to get like the results that are actually accurate... i won't do it if not anonymous.”

explanation: A lecturer shared feedback results and attached action items to each point, making responses specific and usable.
quote: “the following week, she actually kind of shared the results... every single point she actually made sure to like have an action item.”

explanation: More frequent feedback opportunities help students pause and identify what is bothering them, rather than only reacting later.
quote: “having more frequent feedbacks helps. because it also makes me think about what i feel like i take a moment to like, stop and think.”

explanation: Students cannot act on feedback or discuss marks when they are told to contact a marker whose identity is not provided.
quote: "contact your marker... ‘i have no idea who my marker is, because there's no name’"
subtheme: Clear feedback ownership and contact routes

code: Perceived unfair marking needs reliable moderation
explanation: Students discuss mass complaint over marks that seemed unfair relative to other tutorial groups, highlighting concern about consistency of assessment feedback.
quote: "graded unfairly in proportion to like the marks that everyone in other groups got... the moderation hasn’t come back yet"
subtheme: Fairness through moderation and marking alignment

explanation: Strict limits on office hours and email responses can leave students without a practical route to obtain feedback or clarification.
quote: "he's not going to answer any emails about the working hours... he's not going to give any more feedback than he has to"

explanation: Students stop completing surveys because constant feedback requests feel burdensome and low priority, even though they know this reduces voice.
quote: "survey fatigue... i'm just tired of filling them out. so i just don't anymore... it’s not the priority"

code: Feedback invitations need to be visible and accessible
explanation: Student suggests that feedback opportunities should be better advertised rather than hidden in announcement pages, so more students can find and use them.
quote: “make it more well known that there are these surveys and encourage students to fill them up more, rather than just just putting it on the announcement page on learn because students have to be pretty on top of their stuff and know where to find it”

code: Multiple distribution methods support wider participation
explanation: Student supports combining in-class and email feedback methods, making the process easier for both attending and absent students.
quote: “i think both is kind of a good solution. because if you're doing it in class, it's much easier to just fill out a single card... and then like, obviously, if you're not in class... then having emails.”

explanation: Automated emails and announcements become overwhelming, making it less likely that students notice feedback requests; feedback systems need to be clear and manageable.
quote: “we have automated emails too. but it's to the point where they're so flooded that people don't check them a lot. because professors release, like, 20 announcements at the same time”

code: Perceived care from staff increases feedback engagement
explanation: Students are more willing to provide feedback when organisers appear genuinely interested, suggesting the interpersonal framing of feedback affects participation.
quote: “yeah, i think definitely, when it seems like they care, it's a lot more easier to give feedback.”

code: Email as sole feedback route can feel intimidating
explanation: Student notes that emailing staff directly can be intimidating and suggests an anonymous suggestion-box style mechanism, implying feedback channels should be accessible and low-pressure.
quote: “having email as the kind of only ongoing way to give feedback kind of makes it more intimidating. if there was some way to have a kind of suggestion box, but maybe online, would be easier.”

explanation: Student identifies inconsistency across tools and applications as a barrier, arguing that a single standardised system would make giving feedback easier to locate and complete.
quote: “there are so many different applications used that sometimes it would be easier to just use one. so it would be easy for students to find and do.”

explanation: Students prefer having both anonymous and identifiable feedback options, depending on whether the issue is personal or whether a response would be useful.
quote: “i think having both as an option is pretty important. because a lot of the time when it's maybe something less serious, it's better if you get a response. but then sometimes you would rather be anonymous.”

explanation: Student defines effective feedback as receiving a response or acknowledgement, even when the requested change cannot happen immediately.
quote: “seeing the demonstrator or whoever respond either publicly or privately is pretty important. even if it's not something that can be changed until next semester... it's still good to know they've acknowledged it”

code: Addressing feedback through practical teaching changes
explanation: Student describes effective feedback as not only being acknowledged but also producing visible adjustments in teaching practice.
quote: “acknowledging it... but also making slight differences in class and in the way they teach could... or addressing the feedback, in a way, is good.”

code: Partial solutions are valued when exact requests are not possible
explanation: Student recognises that staff may not be able to implement feedback exactly but values compromise actions that respond to the underlying issue.
quote: “even if they can't do exactly what you suggest, then kind of working to do something that's in the middle of what they can do.”

explanation: A student described a previous system where multiple peers needed to identify a free rider before marks were affected, making outcomes feel more reliable.
quote: s1: "it had to be unanimous for that person's mark to go down."

explanation: Students felt that large class sizes make it harder for staff to observe individual contributions and student needs, reducing the reliability of assessment and feedback.
quote: s1: "small classrooms, it's easier for professors to see."

explanation: Students described classrooms that could not accommodate the number of learners, making participation and note-taking difficult.
quote: s1: "it couldn't accommodate all of us and we had to sit in chairs where didn't have... the laptop table... it was very inconvenient."

explanation: Students struggled to identify or contact programme representatives, limiting the accessibility of feedback channels.
quote: s2: "i've been looking in eusa how to find it. i don't know... i can never find them."

explanation: A former representative suggested a clearer Learn area or communication route so students can raise issues with reps more easily.
quote: s2: "they should be able to post or have like, learn, a specific area for reps"

code: Learning concerns should inform assessment weighting
explanation: Students argued that if feedback shows a topic was poorly taught, assessment emphasis should be adjusted rather than penalising students for a teaching problem.
quote: "if you know that majority of the students... pig was not taught really well. you wouldn't put heavy weighted marks on it. because if the course itself is the issue, you can't really hold that against the students"
subtheme: Alignment between teaching quality and assessment expectations

explanation: The ability to give feedback depended on whether specific course staff created an environment where students felt able to speak, making the experience inconsistent.
quote: "it depends on whether or not that course makes you feel open up to talk because i know some of the reps are saying that they didn't particularly feel open to talk"
subtheme: Consistency of psychological safety across courses

explanation: Students at the distant campus did not know who to contact at the main University, suggesting feedback routes were opaque and unreliable beyond the school level.
quote: "if it’s related to the main uni, not only do i not know who to email i don't even know if i'm allowed to email"
subtheme: Clear routes for escalation and communication

explanation: Students recognised the need for decision-making processes but felt over-complex feedback systems prevented timely and meaningful change.
quote: "all the feedback systems are so complex... don't over complexify that it takes years for anything to actually happen."

explanation: Students noted that feedback mechanisms tend to elicit complaints more than positive comments, because students focus on what they want changed.
quote: "i'm also like much more likely to complain that i am to praise, i guess you’ll also underrepresent the good stuff."
subtheme: Capturing positive as well as negative feedback

explanation: Exam feedback consisting only of marks or scores per question is not actionable because it does not explain what was wrong or how to improve.
quote: “exams feedback... would be just a number. and sometimes it's your score per question, but it's just the number you got per question”

explanation: A positive example of useful assessment feedback is when the marker comments on each question and explains why points were awarded.
quote: “the lecturer was the one who marked my paper. and then she wrote a comment for each questions and said, ‘why you got this point’”

explanation: Students value feedback that makes assessment decisions visible, such as comments explaining where marks came from rather than opaque scores.
quote: “for math ones, we also got the assessments back, and i said this one, how many points we got”

explanation: Anonymity is important because power imbalances and concern about hurting staff feelings can prevent honest feedback; this is relevant to feedback conditions but not directly captured by the other themes.
quote: “when it is anonymous, you can be as honest as possible... especially if the lecturer would eventually find out and that's someone who has so much power over the students”

explanation: Focus groups are seen as effective because they provide a safer space for students to express concerns, although safety/anonymity is not directly represented in the specified feedback themes.
quote: “focus group would be the most effective... at least we are given the opportunity to... express your views and that they are heard”

explanation: Non-anonymous or named feedback can increase pressure, particularly for students already managing language barriers and academic workload.
quote: “if you change that feedback, form to label with name, i really feel stressful… makes me like less likely to process this kind of information. and not so good at giving feedback.”

explanation: Individual conversations were experienced as more helpful than impersonal forms because they allowed support to be tailored to the student’s needs.
quote: “not a feedback form, just in the lecturer. they'll chat with us individually. i think that's made to personalize our study method, and i quite enjoy doing so.”
subtheme: Personalised support and tailored next steps

explanation: A staff member identified difficulty during a practical session and proactively contacted the student, providing timely support before the student had to request it.
quote: “they find me not doing the things so well as other students… another staff sent me an email… if i have any difficulties, just tell her. i think it's, they reach out for me”

explanation: Cultural differences and fear of being judged can prevent students from seeking feedback or support, making sensitive communication important.
quote: “at the very beginning of starting here, i was too scared of asking for help, because i'm still afraid of getting of being judged.”

explanation: Students define effective institutional feedback as leading to changes that improve the student experience, not merely being collected.
quote: “make sure other students can benefit from the policy change, and improve our experience of studying here.”

explanation: Effective feedback requires communication that reassures students their input has been noticed and considered.
quote: “make sure students know that you’re making a lot of students, know, all feedback is actually being heard.”

explanation: Some teaching staff are perceived as using expert-level language that students cannot easily interpret, showing the need for feedback and teaching communication to match learner experience.
quote: “these professors… are professionals with 30-40 years of experience… we just sit there like, ‘whoah’… some professors do really well, just talking in students language… but some struggle.”

explanation: Students experience some teaching as large amounts of information being delivered without sufficient structuring or usable resources, making it harder to act on learning needs.
quote: “they overload… every time in the lecture they’re like, okay, here a bunch of drugs… not a handout… why don't you like make it more integrated”

explanation: Students are unsure where submitted feedback goes and how it is processed, which undermines transparency in the feedback system.
quote: “i don't really know how all this information is being processed, we just get sent the link.”

explanation: Written summaries of questions and staff responses are valued because they make the feedback process visible and understandable.
quote: “every time when our class reps have a meeting with the teaching staff… they will send us a document about the question and their response. i think that's quite nice.”

explanation: A confirmation that a form was submitted does not meet students’ needs for meaningful information about what will happen next.
quote: “i filled out the online referral form and then i just didn't hear back from them… i got like a confirmation saying ‘you filled the form out’. but that doesn't do me any good. i know i filled the form out.”

code: Complaints and appeals give inconsistent jurisdictional advice
explanation: Students receive contradictory guidance about whether an issue belongs to complaints or appeals, undermining trust and consistency in the feedback system.
quote: “i had actually submitted a complaint twice. however, they were like, oh, this is actually the appeals jurisdiction… they both emailed me back, and they're like, oh, yeah, you’re right, actually you can't submit a complaint about this… what am i supposed to do?”

code: Staff give conflicting or misleading information
explanation: Participants attribute misinformation to poor internal communication and lack of shared knowledge across the institution.
quote: “they will say, misleading information… i've spoken to several other people where that's just not true… since nobody's in the know, everybody's confused. and they might just be giving you false information.”

explanation: Students define effective feedback as producing a response and tangible action rather than polite acknowledgement without change.
quote: “take action, please. there needs to be some kind of response when somebody complains… they just are like, okay, we will look into it. and then nothing, after that.”

code: Acknowledgement and next steps matter when action is not immediate
explanation: Even if an issue cannot be solved immediately, students want feedback to be acknowledged and moved to a named forum or decision-maker.
quote: “at least they should first acknowledge that they receive the feedback… secondly… we will see what step we can do. at least they could say, we will talk about this in the next school meeting… we will just do something that will maybe move this concern forward.”

explanation: Students report long delays before staff send promised emails or escalate issues, reducing timeliness and leaving students to chase responses.
quote: “after like a week, i was like, hey, so have you heard anything… silence for five days… ‘no, i haven't quite done that yet. but i'll chase them up’… why did this take an extra two weeks just for you to send this email?”

explanation: Students propose a dedicated hub that can answer questions and direct feedback to the correct place, improving clarity and accessibility.
quote: “if i had a magic wand, i would create a hub where things are answered… a hub that specifically specialises in feedback… people who are hired, you know, so they have to show up and do it.”

code: Need institutional accountability for feedback resolution
explanation: Students want an ombudsman or oversight role to monitor whether feedback has been addressed and chase staff rather than leaving students to do so.
quote: “there is no accountability… it would be interesting maybe to have… some sort of ombudsman… someone that can actually say, what has been done about this?… instead of you chasing them, there should be someone at the university chasing the people to answer to you.”

explanation: Students experience the need to chase feedback responses as an inappropriate burden because their primary role is to study.
quote: “because we're supposed to be studying. we can't be, you know, sending emails every hour.”

code: Representatives heard only when staff choose to respond
explanation: Student representative structures exist, but students believe the university is not required to respond to them, making feedback dependent on individual goodwill.
quote: “we have student representatives… but i think nobody at the university is actually taking into account what they are saying. and because there is no accountability… some things have been resolved… not because they have to.”

explanation: Concerns about being identified or treated differently by lecturers may stop students from formally giving feedback, even when they discuss issues with peers. This concern is relevant to participation but not directly captured by the provided feedback-quality themes.
quote: "that's why a lot of the times, we might discuss it among ourselves... but not share it with lectures because we feel it's... a bit harsh, or they'll treat us differently."
subtheme: Psychological safety and anonymity in feedback-giving

explanation: Students experience large organisations as passing problems between departments rather than taking ownership of feedback or issues raised. This is about institutional responsiveness rather than a specific feedback-quality feature in the provided themes.
quote: "a lot of departments are like pushing the question around... they will say, like, this is not our problem, please email another. so they will just push the whole question around, instead of... make a change."

explanation: Students repeatedly describe being asked for feedback but not being shown what happened as a result, making the process opaque and reducing trust.
quote: "the university asks for a lot of feedback in more different ways. but we don't normally see the results of it"

explanation: A lack of visible response makes feedback feel as though it disappears without impact, highlighting the need for clear evidence that student input is received and used.
quote: "it literally is just like sending the form back into the void and nothing ever happens"

explanation: One course made feedback transparent by summarising student comments and reporting back by section, allowing students to see what had been said.
quote: "in the like, really organised course, they had a whole table and summarize the feedback for each different section"

explanation: Students valued when staff returned shortly after feedback closed and explained their specific reaction to comments, making the process visible.
quote: "came back a few days after the format close and showed us how what people said and what their reaction specific reaction is"

explanation: Students identify acknowledgement of receipt and understanding as a core requirement for effective feedback, even where change may take longer.
quote: "the first step to get a response"; "acknowledging that they receive feedback, and that they understand where you're coming from"

explanation: Students want the university to explain what it will do in response to feedback, rather than merely collecting comments.
quote: "show acknowledgment from the university that they're seeing our feedback actually acting on it... these are the steps that we're going to take"

explanation: Effective feedback is described as staff stating what will be changed and what will not be changed, giving students concrete information about outcomes.
quote: "they develop positive and negative and they sort of put a point of what they would change or would not change"

explanation: Students found broad or vague staff responses ineffective because they did not clearly address the specific issues raised or provide a useful route for improvement.
quote: "then they gave up very vague like, oh, so people said, maybe it'd be better if we wrote on a piece of paper"

code: Rapid poll led to deadline extension
explanation: A short poll about coursework difficulty resulted in a concrete deadline extension, which students experienced as feedback being acted on meaningfully.
quote: "given the feedback that we've received on this poll... we decided to extend the deadline... it was the first time i've seen it implemented and acted on"

explanation: Students want follow-up questions to ask whether a precise change has worked, supporting concrete adjustment rather than vague discussion.
quote: "very specific questions in response, saying like, didn't you do this exact thing... like actual specific stuff"

code: Clear directions to staff offices matter
explanation: Even when office hours exist, unclear locations create barriers to accessing feedback conversations.
quote: "it can be difficult to find where it is... there should be more clear directions to get there"

explanation: Students want feedback questions designed around the actual course rather than broad generic items, so responses are more meaningful.
quote: "if there were questions that were more specifically tailored to the course, then i would have an easier time... some of them they’re not relevant at all"

explanation: Closed satisfaction scales do not allow students to describe why something worked or did not work, limiting usefulness for improvement.
quote: "satisfied/ dissatisfied... you don't even have like, an opportunity to say why you're dissatisfied or satisfied"

code: Feedback should allow students’ own terms
explanation: Students prefer formats that let them express what matters to them rather than forcing responses into predetermined categories.
quote: "predetermined answers, it doesn't give people a chance to say how they feel on their own terms"

code: Group discussion as alternative to surveys
explanation: Tutorial-based discussion could allow students to build on each other’s views and generate richer, more usable feedback.
quote: "maybe like one tutorial... where we can actually discuss in the whole group, what's worked for us or not"

explanation: One tutor’s practice of asking for feedback and reporting previous comments each tutorial exemplifies continuous feedback and adjustment.
quote: "in every lesson, or every tutorial, she would ask us for any feedback... she would tell us our previous ones"

explanation: Aggregated feedback results would show the scale of problems and make it harder for the university to ignore them.
quote: "if we see... 80% of people... the university will actually have to act upon it"

code: Detailed tutor feedback models better student feedback
explanation: Receiving rich, specific academic feedback encouraged students to provide similarly detailed feedback to staff, suggesting feedback quality can be reciprocal.
quote: "my tutor was very generous in her feedback... explained why things went right, why things went wrong... [so we] give specific examples"

explanation: When students receive only evaluative comments such as good/bad, they mirror that low engagement in their own feedback.
quote: "when we get feedback like, ‘oh, this is good, this is bad’... they're not engaged. so why should we be"

code: FAQ could clarify course design rationale
explanation: Students suggest advance explanation of why a course is organised a certain way, enabling more informed and goal-referenced feedback.
quote: "have an faq... ‘this is a reason why we organise it in this way’... when we actually give the feedback, then we also have that in mind"

explanation: Students propose a buddy system with regular informal check-ins to ensure everyone has an opportunity to give feedback.
quote: “a buddy system where like you are assigned a buddy... once a week or once a month, you just catch up... do you have any issues... then maybe they can pass on some sort of feedback to the bigger system.”

explanation: Set meetings reduce the pressure of initiating feedback only when there is a problem and make it easier to raise concerns.
quote: “it's really nice to have like a set meeting with your supervisor... it gives you a less pressured moment to be like... this has been bothering me.”

explanation: Students want ongoing feedback structures above the programme level, such as school-level mechanisms, to address broader issues.
quote: “i think that's really nice. really nice if like, the uni would do something like that for school... something higher than just the program.”

explanation: Talking in person with programme leaders is seen as more effective and humanising than anonymous written complaints.
quote: “it has more effect when you talk in person with... the director of the programme, or the course organiser... it's more empathy too.”

explanation: Students perceive effective feedback use as discussion and acknowledgement, even when institutional change is slow.
quote: "i don't really expect them... immediately change... but i would like to see some kind of dialogue... students to know that our feedback is being discussed"

code: Multiple feedback routes support different needs
explanation: Students want both anonymous and in-person channels so feedback methods fit different comfort levels and circumstances.
quote: "having kind of like both ways so that you can decide which one you prefer, whether you prefer to go in person... or whether you prefer anonymity"

code: Fear of repercussions limits direct feedback
explanation: Face-to-face feedback can be difficult when students worry that critical comments may affect marking, tutorials, or relationships with staff.
quote: "we kind of will not give a personal feedback... we all fear how it's going to impact on us... there might be some repercussions"

explanation: Students may not feel authorised to give feedback unless lecturers clearly invite it and indicate when it is welcome.
quote: "the tutors or lecturers don't really ever make clear that they want feedback... i never really felt that i was in a position to give them feedback"

code: Too frequent requests can be overkill
explanation: Repeated requests for feedback in consecutive lectures may overwhelm students if insufficient time has passed for meaningful change.
quote: "when they do it the next lecture as well... what has changed that more people would give feedback like this a bit overkill"

explanation: Students perceive feedback as more effective when teaching teams are engaged, communicative, and passionate about student experience.
quote: "they were actually talking to us, and were sending out emails... everyone on the team was super passionate about the course, and our student experience"

code: Lack of tutorial response creates inequity
explanation: When raised issues about absent online tutorials were not acted on, students lost opportunities to improve through discussion compared with other groups.
quote: "we raised the issue with the course organiser and so on, and nothing was done about it... we didn't get the chance to discuss anything at all"

code: Listening and justification can be enough
explanation: Students emphasise that effective feedback use may involve acknowledging concerns and explaining the rationale behind current practice.
quote: "all i really want is like an explanation... ‘okay, i hear you, but this is why it's done like that’... way more effective than just not responding"

code: Office hours enable timely issue resolution
explanation: Regular office hours allow students to raise problems soon after they occur rather than waiting for mid- or end-semester surveys.
quote: "every week, so if something happens in a particular week, we can go and talk to them... rather than have to wait until the end of the semester"

explanation: Students need clear and accurate information about how to contact staff; otherwise feedback channels are inaccessible.
quote: "some of the information is either outdated or not there at all... be sure that the information that's there is actually correct"

explanation: Students report that feedback returned near the end of semester leaves insufficient time for changes to benefit the current cohort.
quote: "they got back to us, have three weeks left. so there's not enough time to implement the changes"
subtheme: Early enough to benefit current students

explanation: Students suggest feedback should happen earlier in the course, around weeks two to four, so that changes can be made while the course is still running.
quote: "they took the feedback, maybe like week four... at least it's earlier on... for a course that does need to change. i think that's really good to have earlier in the year"
subtheme: Early enough to benefit current students

explanation: A student staff committee occurring in week six or seven meant early problems could not be addressed promptly.
quote: "the student staff committee... ended up happening like about the sixth or seventh week... some problems that i encountered early on, could be resolved early on, which was a little bit annoying"
subtheme: Early enough to benefit current students

explanation: Students valued feedback mechanisms that produced responses within hours, while the issue was still current and actionable.
quote: "it took like, two minutes... three hours later, the professor was like... we decided to extend the deadline"

code: End feedback does not help current learner
explanation: Students feel end-of-course feedback may benefit future cohorts but provides no chance for current students to recover from poor learning experiences.
quote: "it feels sort of worthless to say at the very end what the issues have been... it's also not going to help you"
subtheme: Feedback that supports the current cohort

explanation: Students describe effective feedback as a cycle: receive feedback, communicate a plan, implement changes, then check back later.
quote: "have an overview of like, down the line to check with us like two weeks later to show what changes have been made"

code: Weekly small issues plus larger review
explanation: Students distinguish between frequent feedback for immediate small adjustments and larger feedback for structural course issues, showing a preference for an ongoing feedback cycle.
quote: "weekly forms... getting small details across... and then maybe have one big feedback at the main point or end"

explanation: A continuously available course feedback form would allow students to raise issues when they arise rather than waiting for a scheduled survey.
quote: "it would be good if there was just one, constantly open, sort of general feedback form for me for each course"

explanation: A student imagines scheduled mid-course personal contact using attendance, submission, and grade data to support students before problems become entrenched.
quote: "a scheduled zoom call or telephone call halfway through... access to the data of... late submissions... grades... have an individual discussion about where things might have gone wrong"

explanation: Students feel overwhelmed by the quantity of feedback requests, which reduces engagement and makes the feedback process less accessible.
quote: "it's an overload. the fact is that university as a whole is asking for far too much feedback all the time"

code: Feedback system should not rely on students alone
explanation: Students value peer representatives but argue that formal university staff must also be responsible for dealing with feedback and problems.
quote: “there are representatives and stuff, but it shouldn't be on the students… there needs to be someone who's at the university.”

code: Broader welfare and financial hardship concerns
explanation: Participants discuss financial strain, accommodation insecurity, childcare costs, and lack of support; these are important student experience issues but are not directly about the qualities of feedback itself.
quote: “there needs to be actual services that are open, public, and give us actual services that are related to stuff like, you know, being a student parent… not as students but as individuals, feel cared for.”
subtheme: Wider student support and wellbeing needs

explanation: Students want the University to explicitly acknowledge feedback received and show what has changed as a result, rather than leaving students uncertain about impact.
quote: “there's a lot of times where i feel like the need for the teaching staff to go ‘we've heard your feedback. and this is what we've done to help like the students and stuff. i feel like we don't get that enough.”

explanation: Course feedback is perceived as improving the curriculum for later students, but not always benefiting those who gave the feedback.
quote: “all teaching staff will change accordingly to current students feedback for next years students. that's kind of like an integrated system for all the juniors”

explanation: Midterm feedback is valued because it allows staff to adapt teaching while the current cohort can still benefit.
quote: “we have the midterm feedback, you just allow the staff to hear what we are thinking and adjust the way of teaching so our current student will still benefit from the last half of the teaching. i think that is good.”

explanation: Students perceive staff as repeatedly switching between options based on successive cohorts’ preferences, suggesting a lack of stable criteria for decisions.
quote: “teaching staff just bounce from a to b, b, back to a to b, because that's what students want… last year, students like you don't have enough time for practical… they gave us like an extra hour… this is just way too long… it's gonna go back”

explanation: Students feel that recurring transport feedback is acknowledged but not resolved or visibly progressed, reducing trust in the feedback process.
quote: “we have had a lot of townhall meetings addressing this issue… a lot of our issues are just being like, we can't do a lot of things... we can't do anything about it. and we just feel like the students are not being heard.”
subtheme: Visible action and progress on recurring issues

explanation: Where problems involve external organisations, students still want the University to explain what has been attempted and what negotiations have achieved.
quote: “if you can't like at least try to, like negotiate with lothian buses and they come back to students and like how much have gone through to give students like the reassurance that okay, the university is here for people”
subtheme: Transparency about constraints and external negotiations

explanation: Students can see recurring issues raised in meetings, but visible discussion alone is insufficient without action or evidence of progress.
quote: “every meeting that you can see ‘bus, bus, bus’ , so it’s definitely being addressed… the student union put on like a whole google docs form… what can we do to bring it there.”

explanation: Survey questions are seen as focusing on modules rather than wider student wellbeing and campus experience, limiting the usefulness of student responses.
quote: “it's mostly just on the course, like, how do you feel about animal module 4? they don't ask, how are you spending your time at uni? like, how do you think that facilities improve?”

explanation: The participant distinguishes between collecting feedback and making practical changes, stating that feedback feels heard but not acted upon.
quote: “i feel like yes, the students voices are being heard but not being acted on. ‘okay, we hear you’”
subtheme: Translating student voice into practical change

explanation: Feedback mechanisms may be less usable for non-native English speakers, who may need more accessible formats or language support to participate fully.
quote: “is it possible for surveys to be more inclusive for international students so that they actually will really participate in the survey?… personally, i'm not a native speaker by english and i struggle a bit with english. sometimes i’ll see, but won’t do, a survey.”
